sections.history: Tiruvenpakkam lies in the Tondai country of northern Tamil Nadu, in the Tiruvallur district. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the Shiva shrines sung by the Tevaram saints, and its hymn is remembered as Sundarar's, which carries the shrine's fame back to the age of the Nayanmar saints. The old town, known in the hymns as Tiruvenpakkam and remembered also as Pazhampathi, stood by the waters of the Kuchasthalai. Tradition holds that the original complex was raised in the Chola age, while the masonry temple that followed is placed in the sixteenth century. When the Poondi reservoir was built across the river, the temple was moved in 1942 to its present site on the northern bank at Poondi, and it is carried in worship there to this day.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east in the Dravidian manner, a modest walled shrine rather than a towering complex, standing now on the northern bank of the Poondi reservoir. In the sanctum Shiva is worshipped as Oondreeswarar in the form of the linga. Before the sanctum stands Nandi, the sacred bull, whose image here is shown with a broken horn in memory of the temple's great legend. The goddess Minnoli Amman, whose name is read as the mother of lightning, is enshrined in her own shrine within the walls. Because the present structure was raised in the sixteenth century and rebuilt again on its move in 1942, much of the fabric is later work, though the sanctity and the story it keeps reach back to the Tevaram age.
sections.legends: The defining story of Tiruvenpakkam is Sundarar's. The saint, having lost his sight, came to this place and sang to the Lord for his vision. Shiva gave him a staff, an oondru-kol, to lean on as he walked, and from this gift the Lord is called Oondreeswarar. Still unable to see, and not knowing whose hand had given him the staff, the saint cast it aside in his distress, and it struck the horn of Nandi, which the temple's bull bears broken to this day. As Sundarar set out again, the goddess, who had been kept from walking at his side, sent before him a flash of lightning to show the way, and from this she is honoured as Minnoli, the lightning mother. By tradition the saint's sight was restored to him afterward at Kanchipuram and at Tiruvarur. These accounts are carried in the temple's Sthala Purana and in the lives of the saints.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, falls in the Tamil month of Masi (February–March) and is the foremost observance. In Aipasi (October–November) the temple keeps Annabhishekam, when the linga is adorned with cooked rice, and in the month of Karthikai (November–December) the festival of lights, Tirukarthikai, is kept. An annual Brahmotsavam is also observed. Because the dates follow the Tamil calendar and local custom, confirm them with the temple before a visit.
sections.experience: Tiruvenpakkam rewards an unhurried visit as a quiet country shrine on the bank of the Poondi reservoir, away from the crowds of the larger pilgrim centres. Enter through the eastern gateway, come before the linga of Oondreeswarar in the sanctum, and pause before the Nandi with its broken horn, where the story of Sundarar and his staff feels close at hand. Turn then to the goddess Minnoli in her own shrine, remembered for the lightning that lit the blind saint's path. The open water and fields around the temple lend the place a stillness in keeping with its long history.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands at Poondi, on the northern bank of the Poondi reservoir, on the Tiruvallur–Tiruttani road about 11 km from Tiruvallur, which is the nearest railway junction. Chennai, with the region's international airport, is around 60 km away. Buses along the Tiruvallur–Tiruttani road serve Poondi.
